name: What Are Conditional Statements
html:
Welcome back, dear reader. So, today we are going to learn about conditional statements.


Important Links : Introduction Video

Concept Explanation:

Dear reader, here we will study about conditional statements . Let us not waste any time and dive right into the concept.

Concept of Conditional Statement:

Till now, we have been doing simple programs in which all the lines of the code got executed. Now, we will learn something new. Let us say that we want to learn whether a number is even or odd and print the same. So, if the number is even, we print that the number is even else we print odd.

So, read the above statement again. Yes, you have got the correct hint. If and Else is something which we can use in Java to achieve this. The syntax for if-else is as follows:

So, inside the round brackets, we have some condition. This can be either true or false. If the condition is true then the code inside the if block executes otherwise the code inside the else block executes. For instance, the code for finding whether a number is EVEN or ODD is shown below:

import java.util.*; public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { int x = 10; if (x % 2 == 0) { System.out.println("The number is even"); } else { System.out.println("The number is odd"); } System.out.println("Hardwork is better tahn smart work"); } }
java; true";

The output for the above code is:

What if the number was not 10 but 11? The output for that case is shown below:

As you can see, it prints the first line according to the condition but the line "Hardwork is better than smart work" is always printed whether a number is even or odd because it is not inside any conditional statement.

So, this is the simple example of If-Else statements in Java. Now, do you know that 0 is neither even nor odd?

But, according to this program that we have written above, it will display that 0 is even. Why? Think!!

So, what can we do to make sure that for 0 our output is "Neither Even Nor Odd."

Nested If-Else

Have a look at the program given below:

import java.util.*; public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { int x = 11; if (x % 2 == 0) { if(x == 0) { System.out.println("Neither Even Nor Odd"); } else { System.out.println("The number is even"); } } else { System.out.println("The number is odd"); } System.out.println("Hardwork is better than smart work"); } }
java; true";

So, what are we doing here? We know that 0 on getting divided by 2 will give the remainder 0. So, we will enter the if block. Inside that if block, we can have either the number 0 or any other even number.

So, inside the outer if block, we have written another if-else block which checks whether the number is zero or not. If the number is 0, it prints "Neither Even Nor Odd" else it prints the same as above code.

There is another way to do so. What is it? It is called the If-Else If---Else block. What do we mean by this? Have a look at the code given below:

If-Else If- Else
import java.util.*; public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { int x = 11; if (x == 0) { System.out.println("Neither even Nor Odd"); } else if (x % 2 == 0) { System.out.println("The number is even"); } else { System.out.println("The number is odd"); } System.out.println("Hardwork is better than smart work"); } }
java; true";

So, as shown above, we can use multiple else if statements too. We first check whether the value is 0. If it is, we print the underlying statement and straight away move to the last line else if it is even, we execute the statement inside the else if block else that inside the else block followed by the last statement.

So, dear reader, we hope that you have understood the complete topic. If you still have any doubts, we recommend you refer to the Conditional Statements Video to clear them.
